segments.t: Still in the mayor's office, a moment later. Last time, Samson, the bully from Arkady's childhood, came to ask for a better job, and Arkady talked him into phoning his boss and quitting on the spot. Now Samson wants to know when he starts, and Arkady has one small condition. We'll hear it in Russian first; don't worry about catching every word.
Аркаш, ну что скажешь? Когда начинать?
Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
Let's go back through it. Samson has just quit his old job, so he is in a hurry to start the new one.
'Arkasha, so what do you say?' "Chto skazhesh?" literally asks 'what will you say?', while clipped "Arkash" keeps it chummy.
'When do I start?' Literally, 'when to start?' — "kogda" ('when') plus dictionary-form "nachinat" ('to begin') is all Russian needs here. Arkady is all smiles.
'Any time you like.' Literally, 'in any moment' — "v lyuboy moment". Samson doesn't need to be asked twice.
'Right, I'm ready!' "Vsyo" literally means 'all' or 'everything', and at the start of a line it signals 'right, that's settled!'. Then Arkady slips in one more thing.
'There's just one small formality.' "Formalnost" is an easy cognate with English 'formality', softened by "malenkaya" ('little'). Samson is puzzled.
'What formality?' "Kakaya" ends in '-aya' to match feminine "formalnost". Arkady's answer is short.
'Kiss me.' "Potseluy menya" comes from "tselovat" ('to kiss'); in the show he names a much cruder humiliation, which we keep polite here. Samson can't believe his ears.
'What?' "Chego?" is a blunt, streetwise cousin of "chto?" ('what?'), showing instant disbelief. So Arkady reminds him of their childhood.
'Do you remember the toilet in the communal flat?' "Pomnish" ('do you remember?') leads straight into "v kommunalnoy kvartire", where both endings shift after "v" ('in').
Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
'I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.' "Togda" means 'back then', and "yeshchyo potseluyesh" warns 'you'll kiss me yet!'. Samson is amazed.
'What, you remember all that?' "Ty chto" up front expresses stunned 'wait, what?!', followed by "vsyo pomnish?" ('you remember everything?').
'Oh, I remember everything.' Opening with "a" in "a ya vsyo pomnyu" gives a quiet, icy contrast — 'oh, I remember it all'. Samson hopes it's a joke.
'Are you joking?' "Shutish" comes from "shutka" ('a joke'), asking 'are you kidding me?'. Arkady keeps a straight face.
'No. I'm serious.' Russian skips 'am' and uses the '-no' form "seryozno": literally 'I seriously'. Samson explodes.
'No! Never!' "Nikogda!" ('never!') echoes "net!" as Samson lunges forward, while Arkady doesn't even get up.
Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
'Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.' "Ne nado" calmly warns 'don't do that', and "okhrana" means 'security guards'. Right on cue, they step in.
'Please see him out.' Addressing the guards formally, Arkady adds '-te' in "provodite" ('escort him out'). As Samson leaves, one last line lands.
'If you change your mind, come back.' Russian needs no 'if' here: "peredumayesh" ('you'll rethink it') followed by "prikhodi" ('come on over') says it all.
'The job is waiting.' "Dolzhnost" means an official post or managerial position, rather than ordinary "rabota". Let's listen to the whole scene once more.
Аркаш, ну что скажешь? Когда начинать?
Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
That's it for this part: a childhood promise, kept after thirty years. When you watch the episode, listen for Arkady's calm reply about remembering everything; you'll catch it now. See you next time!
